tx.t: In this talk I would like to tell the story of chocolate. Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which first grew in Central and South America.

The Maya and the Aztecs drank a bitter chocolate drink, often with chilli, and sometimes used the beans as money. Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, and people began to add sugar.
The first solid eating chocolate was made by an English company, Fry, in eighteen forty-seven. Milk chocolate was invented by a Swiss man, Daniel Peter, in eighteen seventy-five.

items.title: Ulugh Beg and the Samarkand Observatory

tx.t: Today I would like to tell you about Ulugh Beg, the ruler and astronomer of Samarkand. Ulugh Beg was a grandson of the conqueror Timur, and he ruled Samarkand in the first half of the fifteenth century.
He built a great observatory in Samarkand in the fourteen twenties. Its main instrument was a giant sextant, with a radius of about forty metres.
With it, his team made a catalogue of more than a thousand stars that was used for centuries. His measurement of the length of the year was wrong by less than a minute.

qs.q: When did he build the observatory?

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Brenton. It began in twenty ten with six hundred and thirty-six bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by twenty-one per cent, and on a busy day there were more than six thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: empty stations at rush hour. The council solved it with a mobile app that shows where bikes are available.
Today, a ride costs two pounds fifty-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

too few bikes in the hills
a mobile app that shows where bikes are available

tx.t: Let us begin with the early history of the bicycle. The first machine of this kind was built in eighteen seventeen by a German baron called Karl von Drais, and it had no pedals.

In the eighteen sixties, pedals were fixed to the front wheel, and the machines were nicknamed boneshakers because of their hard wheels. In the eighteen seventies, the penny-farthing had a huge front wheel, which made it fast but dangerous.

The safety bicycle of the eighteen eighties had two wheels of the same size and a chain driving the back wheel. In eighteen eighty-eight, John Dunlop introduced the air-filled tyre, which made riding far more comfortable.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe how honeybees live and why they matter so much to farmers. A single summer hive can contain up to sixty thousand bees, but only one queen.

The queen can lay as many as two thousand eggs in one day. Worker bees live for only about six weeks in summer, and they spend their lives doing different jobs, from cleaning the hive to collecting nectar.

In its whole life, one worker produces only about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey. Bees tell each other where food is by dancing. The angle of the dance shows the direction, and its length shows the distance.

tx.t: Today I would like to outline what glaciers are, and why they matter for sea level. Glaciers cover about ten per cent of the world's land area.
Together, glaciers and ice sheets store about two thirds of the world's fresh water. A glacier forms when snow builds up for many years and is pressed into dense ice.
Since nineteen hundred, the global sea level has risen by about twenty centimetres. This rise is caused partly by melting ice and partly because warm water takes up more space.
